```{r}
notes_theme = theme_minimal(base_size = 14, base_family = "Source Sans 3")
theme_set(notes_theme)

regression_panel <- function(formula, scat.formula = NULL, data, xlab, ylab) {
  mod <- lm(formula, data = data)
  
  aug <- augment(mod)
  
  plot_fit <- makeFun(mod)
  
  if(is.null(scat.formula)) {
    orig_data <- gf_point(formula, data = data, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, color = "#003300")
  } else {
    orig_data <- gf_point(scat.formula, data = data, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, color = "#003300") 
  }
  
  orig_data <- orig_data %>% gf_fun(plot_fit(x) ~ x, color = "#f15a31")
  
  resid_plot <- gf_point(.std.resid ~ .fitted, data = aug, xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Standardized residuals") %>%
    gf_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "#f15a31")
  
  qq_plot <- gf_qq(~.std.resid, data = aug, xlab = "N(0,1) quantiles", ylab = "Standardized residuals", color = "#003300") %>%
    gf_qqline(color = "#f15a31")
  
  (orig_data | resid_plot | qq_plot)
}


bikes_mlr <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual*weekend, data = bikes)

  mutate(type_num = as.numeric(type == "fake"))

news_mod <- glm(type_num ~ title_words + title_has_excl + title_caps_percent, 
                data = news, family = "binomial")

```

## EDA (aggregated data)

First, make an "aggregated dataset" of **empirical logits**: bin `title_caps_percent`, then find the empirical logit for each bin *within each group*

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| echo: true
news_agg <- news |>
  mutate(tcp_bin = cut(title_caps_percent, c(-Inf, 0, 5,  10, 15, Inf))) |>
  group_by(tcp_bin, title_has_excl) |>
  summarize(
    mean_x = mean(title_caps_percent),
    n = n(),
    n_fake = sum(type_num),
    emp_logit = log((n_fake + 0.5) / (n - n_fake + 0.5)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

news_agg
```

::: small
`r sum(news$title_caps_percent == 0)` of the 150 titles have 0% capital letters, so we choose the bins by hand. Only `r sum(news$title_has_excl)` titles have an exclamation point, so some cells are tiny
:::

## Plot empirical log odds

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
gf_point(emp_logit ~ mean_x, color = ~title_has_excl, size = ~n, data = news_agg) |>
  gf_smooth(method = "lm")
```

- Size of the point = number of articles in the bin
- Is there a nonlinear relationship? 
- Do the lines look parallel, or should we try a different lines model?

## Likelihood Ratio Test

In OLS, we used the extra sums of squares $F$-test to compare nested models

For logistic regression, we use a **likelihood ratio test**

::: medium
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

anova(reduced_model, full_model, test = "LRT")
```


```{r}
#| echo: true

reduced_model <- glm(type_num ~ title_words + title_caps_percent, 
                data = news, family = "binomial")

anova(reduced_model, news_mod2, test = "LRT")
```

:::

## Likelihood Ratio Test

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
**Hypotheses:**
:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
$H_0: \beta_i = \beta_j = ... = 0 \quad$ vs. $\quad H_a: \text{at least 1 } \beta \ne 0$
:::
:::

::::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
**Test statistic:**
:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}

$$\Lambda = 2 \log \frac{\text{max likelihood in full model}}{\text{max likelihood in reduced model}}$$
:::
:::

::::

<br>


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
**Reference distribution:**
:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
$\chi^2_{df}$ where $df=$ number of extra terms in the full model
:::
:::

::::


**Idea:** how much did the full model increase the likelihood over the small model? (High likelihood = good, low likelihood = less good)

## What is deviance?

::: medium
For binary logistic regression, the **deviance** of a model is
$$\text{Deviance} = -2 \log L(\text{model})$$
where $L$ is the maximum value of the likelihood

- Deviance plays the role that SSE played in OLS: **smaller = better fit**
- A bigger model always has deviance that is smaller (or the same) as a smaller model
- The LRT statistic is the **drop in deviance**: $\Lambda = \text{Dev(reduced)} - \text{Dev(full)}$
- We use deviance to compare models
:::

## `anova` table

Deviance = $-2 \log L$

::: small

| Resid DF | Resid Dev | Df | Deviance | Pr(>Chi) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|---|
| n - coefs(reduced)| -2 log L(reduced) |  |  |  |
| n - coefs(full) | -2 log L(full) | # extra coefs | $\Lambda$ | p-value |

:::

## Z-test vs LRT 

Test for one coefficient $H_0: \beta_i = 0$ against $H_A: \beta_i \ne 0$: 

- In OLS, the t-test and F-test give *exactly the same p-values* if you are comparing 1 coefficient
- In logistic regression, the z-test and LRT are **not** equivalent
    - Hopefully they are close
    - If not, the LRT is usually more accurate

```{r}
#| echo: false
lrt_p <- function(term) {
  reduced <- update(news_mod, as.formula(paste(". ~ . -", term)))
  anova(reduced, news_mod, test = "LRT")[2, "Pr(>Chi)"]
}

terms <- c("title_words", "title_has_excl", "title_caps_percent")
tibble(term = terms,
       `z-test p-value` = summary(news_mod)$coefficients[-1, "Pr(>|z|)"],
       `LRT p-value` = map_dbl(terms, lrt_p)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

## Separate tests vs. a joint test

Is `title_has_excl` needed at all? 

```{r}
tidy(news_mod2) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "excl")) |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Is `title_has_excl` needed at all? 

```{r}
anova(reduced_model, news_mod2)
```

::: fragment
- Neither term looks useful on its own (both p-values are large)
- But the joint LRT ($d = 2$) has p-value $=$ `r round(anova(reduced_model, news_mod2, test = "LRT")[2, "Pr(>Chi)"], 3)`
- Same as the $F$-test in MLR: individual tests ask whether a term helps *given the others* are in the model; the LRT test asks whether the **combination** helps
:::

## AIC and BIC for logistic regression

The following "information criteria" can be used to compare nested or non-nested models (smaller values are better)

$$IC = \text{Measure of Fit} + \text{Penalty}$$

<br>

$$AIC = -2 \log(L) + 2k$$

<br>

$$BIC =  -2 \log(L) + \log(n) \cdot k$$

where $L$ is the maximized likelihood of the model and $k$ is the number of coefficients (including the intercept). For binary logistic regression, $-2\log(L)$ is the deviance

## In R

```{r}
#| echo: true


AIC(reduced_model, news_mod, news_mod2)

BIC(reduced_model, news_mod, news_mod2)
```
